sense: the future: it will rain, I’ll go

evidence: Plaut. Men. 225c: Jam ego hīc erō.
terms.comment: Latin keeps the future where English slips into the present after “if” and “when”: hōrologium mittam et librōs, sī erit sūdum, “if it’s fine”. For what will be finished first, the future perfect, where English has the present or the perfect: ubi calx cocta erit, when the lime is (has been) burnt. “Won’t”, refusing, is nōlō (see want).

evidence: Cic. Att. 1.12.4: quod in buccam vēnerit scrībitō
terms.comment: For standing instructions, rules and recipes: the “shall” of laws and of Cato’s farm book.

phrases.latin: Redī citō. — Jam ego hīc erō.
phrases.english: Come back soon. — I’ll be right back.

phrases.latin: jam tē vidēbō et quidem, ut spērō, dē viā rēctā ad mē
phrases.english: I’ll see you soon, and, I hope, straight from the road to my house

phrases.latin: hōrologium mittam et librōs, sī erit sūdum
phrases.english: I’ll send the clock and the books if the weather is fine

phrases.latin: quod hodiē nōn est, crās erit
phrases.english: what isn’t here today will be tomorrow

phrases.latin: cibus sum grandium: crēsce et mandūcābis mē
phrases.english: I am food for the grown: grow, and you will eat me

phrases.latin: hoc signī erit, ubi calx cocta erit
phrases.english: this will be the sign that the lime is burnt

phrases.latin: sī rem nūllam habēbis, quod in buccam vēnerit scrībitō
phrases.english: if you have no news, write whatever comes into your head
